title: Amaal Mallik Says a 'Powerful Syndicate' Blocked Him From 60 Bollywood Films — and He's Done Staying Quiet
excerpt: The composer behind some of Hindi cinema's biggest hits claims eight years of systematic blacklisting, threats to his family, and an industry that punishes anyone who won't play the game.
body:
Amaal Mallik has had enough.

On Tuesday, the 34-year-old music composer — the man behind Sooraj Dooba Hain, the M.S. Dhoni: The Untold Story soundtrack, and dozens of Bollywood’s most-streamed tracks — took to Instagram Stories with a message that was part confession, part indictment.

“Big boys in powerful positions have got me out of more than 60 projects,” Mallik wrote. “I’m trying my best for the last eight years, with utmost sincerity and obviously some respectful terms and conditions of working, but sadly it doesn’t work for this place.”

A Musical Dynasty, a Quiet War

Amaal Mallik comes from Bollywood royalty. His grandfather, Sardar Malik, was a veteran composer of Hindi cinema’s golden age. His uncle is Anu Malik. His younger brother, Armaan Malik, is one of the industry’s most popular playback singers. Amaal himself debuted as a composer with Salman Khan’s Jai Ho in 2014 and went on to win four IIFA Awards and two Filmfare Awards before he turned 30.

None of that, he says, has been enough to protect him.

In a longer post on X, Mallik described what he calls a “mixed syndicate of egoistic humans” — a coordinated network of producers, music labels, and unnamed actors who have systematically removed him from film after film since 2019. He claims to have voluntarily rejected about 20 additional projects on ethical grounds, saying “the musician in me wouldn’t be able to respect himself” if he had taken them.

Beyond Nepotism — A Darker Allegation

India’s film industry has weathered wave after wave of nepotism debates, from the Kangana Ranaut era to the reckoning after Sushant Singh Rajput’s death. Mallik’s allegations go further. He isn’t just claiming that insiders get preferential treatment — he’s describing active, organised exclusion.

“There’s a very powerful group of individuals who have made it their mission to keep me away from films — not just specific projects, but cinema altogether,” Mallik wrote. He stopped short of naming names but promised that “accountability would eventually come their way.”

Most alarmingly, Mallik claims the pressure has extended beyond his career. He alleges threats directed at his family members — a claim that, if true, would mark a significant escalation from the garden-variety politicking that most Bollywood insiders describe in private but rarely discuss publicly.

The composer described eight years of “award-worthy politics” that explain his shrinking presence in film soundtracks. Where he once scored multiple major films a year, his recent filmography has thinned considerably despite his commercial track record remaining strong.

The Indie Pivot

For NRI music fans who grew up on Amaal’s film compositions — playing Main Rahoon Ya Na Rahoon on loop in their college dorms in Toronto or driving to Salamat in Houston — there’s a silver lining to his Bollywood exile.

Mallik has increasingly pivoted to independent music releases, available worldwide on Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube, and JioSaavn. “If a film song comes along, wonderful. If not, there’s no need to worry,” he wrote, encouraging fans to explore his growing indie catalogue.

It’s a familiar arc for Indian artists who find Bollywood’s gatekeeping too suffocating: build directly with your audience, bypass the middlemen, and let streaming platforms handle distribution. AR Rahman did it with 99 Songs. Amit Trivedi built Azaadi Records. Now Mallik appears to be charting the same path — not entirely by choice, but with evident resolve.

What This Means

Mallik’s willingness to go public is rare for an artist who has historically been known for professional discretion. Whether his revelations lead to any concrete change in how the Hindi music industry operates is an open question — the system he describes has survived far louder critics.

But for the millions of Indian music fans scattered across the US, UK, Canada, and beyond, the message is clear: the artist isn’t going anywhere. The music just won’t always arrive inside a movie anymore.

Follow Amaal Mallik’s independent releases on Spotify and YouTube.
